opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a distinction that makes a lot of sense organizationally inside a pharma company, but I don't think it maps very cleanly onto what the model actually needs to be good at.

The traditional framing says hit discovery is about finding *something* that binds, a needle in a haystack across a huge chemical space, and lead optimization is about taking that starting point and tuning it for potency, selectivity, ADME properties, and so on. Different teams, different assays, different tools. But from a modeling perspective, both come down to the same core question: given this target and this molecule, what's the structure of the interaction, and how good is it? If your model really understands the physics and chemistry of binding, it should be useful at both ends. If it only works at one end, that's often a sign it's picking up shortcuts rather than learning something general.

There's also a practical reason. If you build a model that's only good at hit finding, you've solved maybe the first few months of a program. The expensive, time-consuming part is all the iteration afterward. And the reverse is true too: if you only help with optimization, you're stuck with whatever starting points people found by brute-force screening, which might not be great chemical matter. Our goal is to compress the whole cycle, so we want something that can propose good molecules from scratch *and* tell you meaningfully which small modifications will help.

And honestly, the line is getting blurrier anyway. When you can design binders computationally with decent hit rates and decent affinities right out of the gate, the "hit" you get is already much closer to a lead. So rather than optimize for one stage, we try to push general capability: accurate structure, accurate ranking, and the ability to generate. Then the stages kind of take care of themselves. If the model is good, people will use it wherever it's useful, and we'd rather not artificially box it in.

astra-6.text:
Because, from the model’s perspective, they’re really the same problem: you’re searching for a molecule that satisfies a set of constraints. In hit discovery, you might start with very little information and search broadly. In lead optimization, you have a molecule that works to some extent, and you want to improve particular properties while preserving others.

We want that to be a continuous process. As you get experimental data, you can condition the model on what you’ve learned and steer the search. Binding is one objective, but you also care about things like specificity and developability. If you treat those as considerations from the beginning, you’re working toward a useful molecule throughout, rather than treating finding a binder as a separate problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of them as the same underlying problem: you’re searching for a molecule that satisfies a set of constraints. In hit discovery, you might care primarily about whether it binds. As you move into lead optimization, you add constraints around potency, selectivity, solubility, and so on. The objectives change, but I don’t think that necessarily calls for a fundamentally different model.

Ideally, you have a model that can take those constraints and reason jointly about the molecule and its interaction with the target. Then finding an initial hit and improving an existing molecule become different ways of using the same capability.
